content: 1. Recreational water safety planning involves identifying existing control measures and determining how risk assessments will be conducted. 2. Risk assessments should be performed, taking into account the effectiveness of current control measures. 3. Control measures that could mitigate inadequately controlled risks must be identified and validated. 4. Improvement plans should be established and prioritized based on the identified risks. 5. Monitoring programs must be planned, specifying who is responsible, what will be monitored, how it will be done, the timing and frequency, sampling locations, and who will analyze and assess the results. Data reporting and storage protocols should also be defined. 6. An initial microbial water quality assessment should determine whether sufficient data exists to classify recreational water based on susceptibility to fecal and chemical contamination, harmful algal blooms (HABs), or free-living microbial pathogens. 7. Monitoring requirements for classifying recreational water bodies should be determined, referencing relevant guidelines. 8. Operational monitoring should identify requirements for priority control measures, establish operational targets and limits to distinguish acceptable from unacceptable performance, and define corrective actions for unacceptable outcomes. 9. Criteria must be established to confirm that acceptable performance of control measures has been restored. 10. Verification involves monitoring indicators of fecal contamination, HABs, and ecotoxicity to confirm the performance of the Recreational Water Safety Plan (RWSP) and ensure stability or improvement in water classifications. 11. Incident response plans (IRPs) should include frameworks for implementing responses, criteria for defining predictable incidents, reporting requirements with timelines, and criteria for issuing and rescinding recreational water closures. 12. A water incident coordinator and mechanisms for establishing incident management teams (IMTs) should be identified, along with the responsibilities of IMT members. 13. Communication protocols must be established to notify recreational water users when necessary. 14. Predictive models should be evaluated for their ability to forecast periods of poor water quality. 15. Rapid monitoring programs should be identified to enable same-day determination of recreational water quality. 16. Supporting programs should be identified to improve control of recreational water bodies, address knowledge gaps, and facilitate RWSP operations. 17. Communication plans should be developed to promote awareness and involvement of recreational water users, especially during incidents and emergencies. 18. All aspects of RWSPs should be documented, including the lead agency, team members, stakeholder responsibilities, system assessments, hazard identification, risk assessments, control measures, improvement plans, operational procedures, monitoring programs, corrective actions, IRPs, supporting programs, and communication protocols. 19. Mechanisms and schedules for regular review of RWSP performance and content should be established. 20. RWSPs and IRPs should be reviewed after significant incidents or emergencies to identify necessary changes. 21. Fecal pollution introduces disease-causing microorganisms into recreational water, primarily from human sewage or excreta from warm-blooded animals. 22. National health-based targets for fecal pollution should be set, considering sources and levels of contamination, health effects, exposure conditions, and host susceptibility. 23. Pathogens and indicator organisms, such as adenoviruses, noroviruses, Campylobacter spp., and Escherichia coli, should be monitored to assess water quality and associated health risks. 24. Sanitary inspection surveys should identify fecal pollution sources to inform beach classification and management actions. 25. Recreational water contamination can arise from human sewage, animal excreta, recreational water users, and runoff from surrounding land. 26. Risks vary with local conditions, such as tidal exchange in estuaries or sediment resuspension in shallow lakes. 27. Animal inputs are generally less significant to human health risk than human excreta but should still be considered during sanitary inspections. 28. Fecal indicator organisms (FIOs), such as intestinal enterococci and E. coli, are commonly used to assess water quality, but their limitations and environmental variability should be acknowledged. 29. Molecular methods, such as quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), are increasingly used for FIO analysis, though standardization and accreditation are essential. 30. Fecal source attribution methods, including microbial source tracking (MST), should be employed to identify contamination sources when unacceptable FIO levels are detected.
